name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q01 - Livestock population and farm produce contribution

questiontext.text: Although India and China together account for more than 70 per cent of the world livestock population, what is their approximate contribution to the world farm produce?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Livestock productivity depends not only on population size but also on breed quality, scientific management, and modern breeding technologies.

Step 2: Evaluation
More than 70 per cent of the world's livestock population is located in India and China, yet their combined contribution to the world farm produce is only 25 per cent, indicating very low productivity per unit.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The contribution of India and China to the world farm produce is 25 per cent.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q02 - Definition of breed in animal husbandry

questiontext.text: In animal husbandry, a group of animals related by descent and similar in most characters such as general appearance, features, size, and configuration is referred to as a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Animal breeding relies on classifying livestock populations based on shared ancestry and phenotypic uniformity.

Step 2: Evaluation
A breed is defined as a group of animals related by descent and similar in most characters like general appearance, features, size, and configuration. A cultivar refers to a cultivated plant variety, a somaclone refers to genetically identical tissue-cultured plants, and an explant is a plant part used to initiate tissue culture.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Such a group of animals is said to belong to a breed.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q03 - Primary factor determining milk yield in dairy farming

questiontext.text: In dairy farm management, milk yield is primarily dependent on which of the following factors?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dairy farm management encompasses processes and systems aimed at increasing milk yield and improving milk quality.

Step 2: Evaluation
While housing, adequate water, scientific feeding, cleanliness, and veterinary visits are essential to realise the yield potential, milk yield is primarily dependent on the quality of breeds in the farm—specifically selecting good breeds with high-yielding potential under local climatic conditions combined with disease resistance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Milk yield is primarily dependent on the quality of breeds in the farm.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q04 - Domesticated birds included under poultry

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups of domesticated fowl is typically included under poultry farm management for food or eggs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Poultry refers to the class of domesticated fowl (birds) used for food or for their eggs.

Step 2: Evaluation
Poultry typically includes chicken and ducks, and sometimes turkey and geese. Crustaceans (prawns, crabs) and molluscs belong to fisheries, while sheep and goats are mammalian livestock.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chicken, ducks, turkey, and geese are the domesticated birds included under poultry.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q05 - Genetic consequences of inbreeding in animals

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes a consequence of inbreeding in cattle over 4–6 generations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inbreeding is the mating of more closely related individuals within the same breed for 4 to 6 generations, following a strategy similar to developing homozygous purelines in peas.

Step 2: Evaluation
Inbreeding increases homozygosity, which is necessary to evolve a pureline in any animal. It also exposes harmful recessive genes that are eliminated by selection, while accumulating superior genes. It does not increase heterozygosity, nor does it involve crossing different species or different breeds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Inbreeding increases homozygosity and exposes harmful recessive genes that are eliminated by selection.

answer.text: It increases homozygosity and exposes harmful recessive genes that are eliminated by selection.
It increases heterozygosity and prevents the formation of purelines.
It involves mating superior males and females belonging to two different related species.
It permanently prevents inbreeding depression regardless of how closely related the mates are.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q06 - Overcoming inbreeding depression in livestock

questiontext.text: When continued close inbreeding in a cattle herd leads to reduced fertility and productivity, what is the recommended breeding measure to restore fertility and yield?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Continued close inbreeding reduces fertility and productivity, a condition known as inbreeding depression.

Step 2: Evaluation
To overcome inbreeding depression, selected animals of the breeding population should be mated with unrelated superior animals of the same breed (a single out-cross). Continuing close inbreeding worsens depression, while interspecific hybridisation or random culling does not restore pure-breed fertility and yield.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mating selected animals with unrelated superior animals of the same breed restores fertility and yield.

answer.text: Subjecting the herd to further close inbreeding for 4–6 additional generations
Mating the affected cattle with a different related species
Mating selected animals with unrelated superior animals of the same breed
Inducing mutations in the cattle using gamma radiations

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q07 - Out-crossing definition and application

questiontext.text: Which breeding method is considered best for animals that are below average in productivity in milk production or growth rate in beef cattle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Out-crossing is the practice of mating animals within the same breed that have no common ancestors on either side of their pedigree up to 4–6 generations.

Step 2: Evaluation
The offspring of such a mating is called an out-cross. It is specifically recognised as the best breeding method for animals that are below average in productivity in milk production, growth rate in beef cattle, and similar traits.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Out-crossing is the best breeding method for below-average animals in milk production or beef cattle growth rate.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q08 - Parentage of Hisardale sheep breed

questiontext.text: Hisardale, a new breed of sheep developed in Punjab through cross-breeding, was obtained by crossing:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cross-breeding mates superior males of one breed with superior females of another breed to combine desirable qualities of two different breeds.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hisardale is a new sheep breed developed in Punjab by crossing Bikaneri ewes (females) and Marino rams (males).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hisardale was developed by crossing Bikaneri ewes and Marino rams.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q09 - Hormone action and embryo recovery stage in MOET

questiontext.text: In Multiple Ovulation Embryo Transfer Technology (MOET), a cow is administered hormones with FSH-like activity to produce how many eggs per cycle, and at which cellular stage are the fertilised eggs recovered non-surgically?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
MOET is a herd improvement programme that increases the reproductive output of high-yielding females using superovulation and surrogate mothers.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hormones with FSH-like activity induce follicular maturation and superovulation, causing the cow to produce 6 to 8 eggs instead of the normal single egg per cycle. After mating or artificial insemination, the fertilised eggs are recovered non-surgically at the 8–32 cell stages and transferred to surrogate mothers.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Superovulation yields 6–8 eggs per cycle, and fertilised eggs are recovered non-surgically at the 8–32 cell stages.

answer.text: 6–8 eggs; recovered at single-celled zygote stage

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q10 - Apiculture species and dual benefits in crop fields

questiontext.text: Which of the following is the most common species of honeybee reared in India, and why are beehives kept in crop fields of sunflower, Brassica, apple, and pear during their flowering period?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apiculture (bee-keeping) involves maintaining hives of honeybees for honey and beeswax, and it also plays a vital ecological role in crop pollination.

Step 2: Evaluation
The most common species of honeybee reared is Apis indica. Honeybees act as pollinators for crops such as sunflower, Brassica, apple, and pear. Keeping beehives in crop fields during the flowering period increases pollination efficiency, thereby improving both crop yield and honey yield.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Apis indica is the most common reared species, and keeping hives in flowering crop fields increases pollination efficiency, improving both crop yield and honey yield.

answer.text: Apis dorsata; to eliminate insect pests from the crops
Apis mellifera; to increase nitrogen fixation in the soil
Apis indica; to increase pollination efficiency, improving both crop yield and honey yield
Apis florea; to prevent fungal rust infections during flowering

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q11 - Classification of common freshwater and marine fishes

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs consists exclusively of common freshwater edible fishes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fisheries involve catching, processing, and selling freshwater and marine fishes as well as shellfish and other aquatic animals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Common freshwater fishes include Catla, Rohu, and common carp. In contrast, Hilsa, Sardines, Mackerel, and Pomfrets are marine fishes eaten by humans.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Catla and Rohu are both common freshwater edible fishes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q12 - Blue Revolution and aquatic food production

questiontext.text: The term 'Blue Revolution', implemented along lines similar to the 'Green Revolution', is associated with increasing the production of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aquaculture and pisciculture techniques have been employed to increase the production of both freshwater and marine aquatic organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
The flourishing of the fishery industry—covering fish, molluscs (such as edible oysters), crustaceans (prawns, crabs, lobsters), and aquatic plants—is referred to as the 'Blue Revolution'.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The 'Blue Revolution' is associated with increasing the production of aquatic plants and animals (fisheries).

answer.text: Fish and other aquatic plants and animals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q13 - Definition of germplasm collection in plant breeding

questiontext.text: In a plant breeding programme, the entire collection of plants or seeds having all the diverse alleles for all genes in a given crop is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic variability is the root of any plant breeding programme and is often obtained from wild relatives and diverse varieties of a crop.

Step 2: Evaluation
Collection and preservation of all different wild varieties, species, and relatives of a cultivated species constitute the germplasm collection—the entire collection of plants or seeds containing all diverse alleles for all genes in that crop.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This entire collection is called the germplasm collection.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q14 - Self-pollination of superior recombinants for homozygosity

questiontext.text: During the step of 'selection and testing of superior recombinants' in plant breeding, why are the selected hybrid progeny plants self-pollinated for several generations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Superior recombinants selected from hybrid progeny often carry heterozygous loci that would segregate in subsequent sexual generations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Self-pollinating the selected superior recombinants for several generations brings them to a state of uniformity (homozygosity) so that the desirable characters will not segregate in the progeny.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Self-pollination is performed until they reach homozygosity so that characters do not segregate in the progeny.

answer.text: To induce artificial mutations in the base sequence of genes
To increase heterozygosity and prevent pureline formation
To achieve uniformity (homozygosity) so that characters will not segregate in the progeny
To digest the cell walls and isolate naked protoplasts

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q15 - Multi-season testing and check cultivar in crop release

questiontext.text: Before a newly bred crop cultivar is released and commercialised in India, it is evaluated in farmers' fields across all relevant agroclimatic zones for at least how many growing seasons, and against what standard is it compared?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Testing, release, and commercialisation of new cultivars require rigorous evaluation first in research fields and subsequently in farmers' fields.

Step 2: Evaluation
After evaluation in research fields under ideal fertiliser and irrigation practices, the material is tested in farmers' fields for at least three growing seasons at several locations representing all agroclimatic zones where the crop is grown. It is compared against the best available local crop cultivar, known as a check or reference cultivar.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Testing is carried out for at least three growing seasons in comparison to the best available local crop cultivar (check or reference cultivar).

answer.text: One growing season; compared against a wild relative
Two growing seasons; compared against an unrelated species
Five growing seasons; compared against a somaclonal variant
At least three growing seasons; compared against the best available local check cultivar

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q16 - Green Revolution wheat and rice production increase

questiontext.text: During the period 1960 to 2000 in India, due to the development of semi-dwarf varieties, wheat and rice production increased respectively from:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Green Revolution in India dramatically boosted cereal production per unit area through semi-dwarf high-yielding varieties.

Step 2: Evaluation
Between 1960 and 2000, wheat production increased from 11 million tonnes to 75 million tonnes, while rice production increased from 35 million tonnes to 89.5 million tonnes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Wheat production rose from 11 to 75 million tonnes and rice production rose from 35 to 89.5 million tonnes.

answer.text: 35 to 89.5 million tonnes (wheat) and 11 to 75 million tonnes (rice)
11 to 75 million tonnes (wheat) and 35 to 89.5 million tonnes (rice)
20 to 60 million tonnes (wheat) and 40 to 100 million tonnes (rice)
11 to 35 million tonnes (wheat) and 75 to 89.5 million tonnes (rice)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q17 - Origins of semi-dwarf rice varieties in India

questiontext.text: The semi-dwarf rice varieties introduced in India in 1966 were derived from which pair of parent varieties?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Semi-dwarf rice varieties played a central role in the Green Revolution in India.

Step 2: Evaluation
The semi-dwarf rice derivatives introduced in 1966 were derived from IR-8 (developed at the International Rice Research Institute, IRRI, Philippines) and Taichung Native-1 (from Taiwan). Later, Jaya and Ratna were developed in India, whereas Sonalika and Kalyan Sona are semi-dwarf wheat varieties.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The semi-dwarf rice varieties introduced in 1966 were derived from IR-8 and Taichung Native-1.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q18 - Hybrid millets resistant to water stress

questiontext.text: Hybrid breeding in India has led to the development of several high-yielding varieties resistant to water stress in which group of crops?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant breeders aim to incorporate tolerance to environmental stresses such as salinity, extreme temperatures, and drought (water stress) alongside high yield.

Step 2: Evaluation
In India, hybrid maize, jowar, and bajra have been successfully developed, and hybrid breeding in these millets has produced several high-yielding varieties resistant to water stress.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
High-yielding, water-stress-resistant hybrids were developed in maize, jowar, and bajra.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q19 - Classification of fungal, bacterial, and viral crop diseases

questiontext.text: Which of the following crop diseases is caused by a bacterium rather than a fungus or a virus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Before breeding crops for disease resistance, it is important to identify the causative pathogen (fungal, bacterial, or viral) and its mode of transmission.

Step 2: Evaluation
Brown rust of wheat, red rot of sugarcane, and late blight of potato are caused by fungi. Tobacco mosaic and turnip mosaic are caused by viruses. Black rot of crucifers is caused by bacteria.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Black rot of crucifers is a bacterial disease.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q20 - Disease-resistant cauliflower varieties

questiontext.text: Pusa Shubhra and Pusa Snowball K-1 are disease-resistant varieties of which crop, and against which diseases are they resistant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hybridisation and selection have produced several disease-resistant crop cultivars against fungal, bacterial, and viral pathogens.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pusa Shubhra and Pusa Snowball K-1 are varieties of cauliflower bred for resistance to black rot and curl blight black rot. In contrast, Pusa swarnim is a Brassica variety resistant to white rust, and Pusa Komal is a cowpea variety resistant to bacterial blight.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pusa Shubhra and Pusa Snowball K-1 are cauliflower varieties resistant to black rot and curl blight black rot.

answer.text: Wheat; resistant to leaf and stripe rust
Cauliflower; resistant to black rot and curl blight black rot

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q21 - Mutation breeding in mung bean

questiontext.text: In mung bean, resistance to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew was induced by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When limited disease resistance genes are available in existing crop varieties or wild relatives, artificial mutations can be induced to generate new desirable traits.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mutation breeding uses chemicals or radiations (such as gamma radiations) to induce changes in the base sequence within genes, followed by screening and selecting resistant plants. In mung bean, resistance to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew was induced by mutations.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Resistance in mung bean to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew was induced by mutation breeding.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q22 - Transfer of yellow mosaic virus resistance in bhindi

questiontext.text: The variety Parbhani kranti of bhindi (Abelmoschus esculentus) is resistant to yellow mosaic virus. How was this resistance gene introduced into A. esculentus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Wild relatives of cultivated plants often carry valuable disease-resistance genes, even though their yields are low.

Step 2: Evaluation
Resistance to yellow mosaic virus in bhindi (Abelmoschus esculentus) was transferred from a related wild species via sexual hybridisation between the target and source plants followed by selection, resulting in the variety Parbhani kranti.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The resistance gene was transferred from a wild species through sexual hybridisation followed by selection.

answer.text: By fusing protoplasts of bhindi with those of mung bean
By transferring the resistance gene from a wild species via sexual hybridisation and selection
By culturing axillary meristems of virus-infected bhindi plants

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q23 - Morphological traits for insect pest resistance in crops

questiontext.text: Which of the following morphological characteristics in host crop plants is associated with resistance to jassids in cotton and cereal leaf beetle in wheat?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Insect resistance in crop plants may be conferred by morphological, biochemical, or physiological characteristics.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hairy leaves in several plants are associated with resistance to insect pests, specifically jassids in cotton and cereal leaf beetle in wheat. Solid stems in wheat deter the stem sawfly, while smooth-leaved and nectar-less cotton varieties do not attract bollworms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hairy leaves confer resistance to jassids in cotton and cereal leaf beetle in wheat.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q24 - Okra varieties resistant to shoot and fruit borer

questiontext.text: Which of the following released varieties of okra (bhindi) are resistant to shoot and fruit borer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hybridisation and selection have yielded crop varieties specifically resistant to major insect pests.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pusa Sawani and Pusa A-4 are varieties of okra (bhindi) resistant to shoot and fruit borer. Pusa Gaurav is a Brassica variety resistant to aphids, while Pusa Sem 2 and Pusa Sem 3 are flat bean varieties resistant to jassids, aphids, and fruit borer.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pusa Sawani and Pusa A-4 are the okra varieties resistant to shoot and fruit borer.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q25 - Hidden hunger and essential micronutrients

questiontext.text: Approximately three billion people worldwide suffer from 'hidden hunger' due to deficiencies of proteins, vitamins, and essential micronutrients. Which set of micronutrients is specifically highlighted as lacking in such diets?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hidden hunger occurs when populations cannot afford enough fruits, vegetables, legumes, fish, and meat, leading to micronutrient, protein, and vitamin deficiencies.

Step 2: Evaluation
Diets lacking essential micronutrients—particularly iron, vitamin A, iodine, and zinc—increase the risk for disease, reduce lifespan, and impair mental abilities. Biofortification is the most practical means to address this.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The essential micronutrients specifically lacking are iron, vitamin A, iodine, and zinc.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q26 - Biofortified vegetable crops released by IARI

questiontext.text: Which of the following combinations of biofortified vegetable crops released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI), New Delhi, and their enriched nutrients is INCORRECT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
IARI, New Delhi, has developed several biofortified vegetable crops enriched with specific vitamins, minerals, or proteins.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Carrots, spinach, and pumpkin are enriched with vitamin A.
2. Bitter gourd, bathua, mustard, and tomato are enriched with vitamin C.
3. Spinach and bathua are enriched with iron and calcium.
4. Broad, lablab, French, and garden peas are enriched with protein, not vitamin C.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Claiming that broad, lablab, French, and garden peas are vitamin C-enriched is incorrect; they are protein-enriched.

answer.text: Carrots, spinach, and pumpkin — Vitamin A enriched
Bitter gourd, bathua, mustard, and tomato — Vitamin C enriched
Broad, lablab, French, and garden peas — Vitamin C enriched

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q27 - Grain requirement for meat production

questiontext.text: Why does a shift from grain-based diets to meat-based diets create a much higher demand for cereals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Energy transfer across trophic levels in a food chain involves substantial loss, meaning producing animal biomass requires much more plant biomass.

Step 2: Evaluation
It takes 3 to 10 kg of grain to produce just 1 kg of meat through animal farming, which greatly amplifies cereal demand when human diets shift toward meat.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Producing 1 kg of meat requires 3–10 kg of grain.

answer.text: Because 1 kg of grain is needed to produce 3–10 kg of meat
Because 3–10 kg of grain is required to produce 1 kg of meat
Because livestock cannot digest cellulose and require only refined sugars
Because meat diets eliminate the need for Single Cell Protein

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q28 - Substrates and environmental benefit of Spirulina SCP

questiontext.text: Blue-green algae like Spirulina can be grown easily on waste water from potato processing plants, straw, molasses, animal manure, and sewage. Besides serving as a food rich in protein, minerals, fats, carbohydrates, and vitamins, what additional benefit does this practice provide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Single Cell Protein (SCP) production utilises industrial and agricultural wastes as growth substrates for microbes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Culturing Spirulina on starch-rich waste water from potato processing plants, straw, molasses, animal manure, and sewage converts waste materials into nutritious biomass and simultaneously reduces environmental pollution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Utilising such waste materials for Spirulina cultivation reduces environmental pollution.

answer.text: It generates somaclones for commercial apple farming
It replaces the need for pollination by honeybees

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q29 - Protein production capacity of Methylophilus methylotrophus

questiontext.text: Which bacterial species, due to its high rate of biomass production and growth, is expected to produce 25 tonnes of protein as a Single Cell Protein (SCP) source?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Microbes with rapid growth and high biomass production rates are ideal candidates for industrial Single Cell Protein (SCP) production.

Step 2: Evaluation
Certain bacterial species like Methylophilus methylotrophus, owing to their high rate of biomass production and growth, can be expected to produce 25 tonnes of protein. Spirulina is a blue-green alga, while Saccharum officinarum and Abelmoschus esculentus are higher plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The bacterial species is Methylophilus methylotrophus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q30 - Fungi as a source of Single Cell Protein

questiontext.text: Why is it considered believable that microscopic fungi could become widely acceptable as human food under Single Cell Protein (SCP) programmes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Single Cell Protein (SCP) explores microbes—including algae, bacteria, and fungi—as alternative protein sources for human and animal nutrition.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because edible mushrooms are already eaten by many people and large-scale mushroom culture is a growing industry, it is believable that microscopic fungi too would become acceptable as food.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The widespread consumption of edible mushrooms and the growing mushroom culture industry support the acceptability of microscopic fungi as food.

answer.text: Because microscopic fungi carry out photosynthesis like blue-green algae
Because microscopic fungi are used to induce superovulation in livestock
Because edible mushrooms are already eaten by many people and large-scale mushroom culture is a growing industry
Because microscopic fungi are the primary pollinators of flowering crops

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q31 - Concept of explant and totipotency in tissue culture

questiontext.text: In plant tissue culture, the capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant grown under sterile conditions in a nutrient medium is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During the 1950s, scientists discovered that whole plants could be regenerated from explants—any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube under sterile conditions in special nutrient media.

Step 2: Evaluation
This capacity of any plant cell or explant to regenerate into a complete whole plant is termed totipotency. Biofortification refers to breeding nutrient-rich crops, inbreeding depression is reduced vigour from close inbreeding, and apiculture is bee-keeping.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant is called totipotency.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q32 - Components of nutrient medium in tissue culture

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly lists the essential components that must be provided in a nutrient medium for plant tissue culture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For an explant to regenerate into a whole plant in vitro, the sterile nutrient medium must supply energy, mineral nutrients, organic supplements, and growth regulators.

Step 2: Evaluation
The nutrient medium must provide a carbon source such as sucrose, along with inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators such as auxins and cytokinins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, auxins, and cytokinins are the required components of the tissue culture medium.

answer.text: Only sucrose and amino acids without any growth regulators
Sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q33 - Micro-propagation and genetic uniformity of somaclones

questiontext.text: Plants produced in thousands through tissue culture micro-propagation—such as tomato, banana, and apple—are called somaclones because they are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Micro-propagation is the method of producing thousands of plants in very short durations through tissue culture.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each plant regenerated through micro-propagation from a somatic explant is genetically identical to the original plant from which it was grown; hence, these plants are called somaclones.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They are called somaclones because they are genetically identical to the original parent plant.

answer.text: Genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown
Produced by fusing naked protoplasts of two different plant species
Obtained exclusively by sexual hybridisation between two purelines

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q34 - Recovery of virus-free plants from diseased crops

questiontext.text: A farmer has virus-infected plants of banana, sugarcane, and potato. Which part of the infected plant should be excised and cultured in vitro to recover healthy, virus-free plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Tissue culture provides an effective method for recovering healthy plants from virus-infected plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Even when a plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (both apical and axillary) remains free of the virus. Removing the meristem and growing it in vitro yields virus-free plants, as successfully demonstrated in banana, sugarcane, and potato.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Apical and axillary meristems should be cultured in vitro to obtain virus-free plants.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q35 - Isolation and fusion of protoplasts in somatic hybridisation

questiontext.text: In somatic hybridisation, what must be removed from isolated single plant cells before fusing them to form hybrid protoplasts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Somatic hybridisation combines desirable traits from two different plant varieties by fusing their somatic cells in vitro.

Step 2: Evaluation
To enable cell fusion, the rigid cell walls of isolated single plant cells must be digested, leaving naked protoplasts surrounded by their plasma membranes. These naked protoplasts from two varieties can then be fused to form hybrid protoplasts.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cell walls must be digested to isolate naked protoplasts prior to fusion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MCQ_Q36 - Evaluation of pomato and somatic hybridisation outcomes

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding the somatic hybrid 'pomato' is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Somatic hybridisation fuses protoplasts from two different plant varieties or species to combine traits from both parents into a single regenerated plant.

Step 2: Evaluation
Protoplasts of tomato and potato were fused and grown to form the somatic hybrid plant named pomato, combining tomato and potato characteristics. However, pomato did not possess all the desired combination of characteristics required for its commercial utilisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pomato was produced by fusing tomato and potato protoplasts, but it lacked all desired characteristics for commercial utilisation.

answer.text: It was produced by sexual hybridisation between tomato and potato and is widely cultivated commercially.
It is a virus-free somaclone obtained by culturing potato meristems in tomato extract.
It was produced by gamma-radiation-induced mutation breeding of potato tubers.
It was formed by fusing protoplasts of tomato and potato, but lacked all desired characteristics for commercial utilisation.
